newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian cen bank says debt plan neutral on budget.
newsitem.headline: Belgian cen bank says debt plan neutral on budget.

text.p: Belgian National Bank (BNB) governor Alfons Verplaetse said in an interview published on Wednesday that government plans to cut the national debt using part of the central bank's foreign exchange reserves would not help toward reducing the 1997 deficit.
"The operation would be neutral on the 1997 budget and subsequent years," Verplaetse told L'Echo newspaper.

Verplaetse said that using the bank's reserves could shave more than 200 billion Belgian francs from the debt, saving Belgium some debt service charges, but added the government would lose interest it currently receives on the reserves.

The Belgian national bank has built up 236 billion francs in reserves from gold sales over recent years. Under a draft law adopted by the government last Friday this "unavailable surplus on capital gains on gold (sales)" could be used to cut the debt.
Verplaetse told L'Echo that a "small part" of the 236 billion was not available because it belongs to Luxembourg under the terms of the two countries' 74-year-old currency union.
The government law also specifies July 1, 1996, as a deadline for valuing the reserve.
Verplaetse told L'Echo he believed the reserves should only be used as part of a wider plan to reduce the debt.

"I expect therefore that that government also takes steps to reduce the debt through other measures...Notably through privatisations. A part of the proceeds from privatisations that have already happened or are to come should be used, I think, to cut the debt," Verplaetse reiterated.

Verplaetse said he believed the government would succeed in bringing Belgium's deficit down to below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), as targeted in the Maastricht Treaty on economic and monetary union (EMU).
"We should be able to get down to a deficit of 2.8 or 2.9 percent at the end of 1997, and 2.5 percent the year after."
The budget is due to be presented to parliament next Tuesday.
